n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.1: The task: from vectors to the next token
n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.2: After module 2 we have one vector per token, x [T, 4096]. Here we simplify to one row per word. The word “{{example_preposition}}” does not yet know its context.
n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.3: To guess the next token, the last position needs to know everything relevant about the whole text: who does what, where, and what usually comes next.
n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.4: That is the job of the rest of the model: fill every token’s vector with context, step by step, until the last one is enough to predict what follows.
n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.5: The thing that does the job is called a transformer: a stack of identical blocks that read and write the same vector per token. The next slides explain the term, then how it is built.
n3c.uppgiften-fran-vektorer-till.8: The illustration uses whole words, with separate rows for articles, not the real BPE boundaries from module 2. The labels describe roughly what the vectors can carry. In the model it is just numbers, and the content is not that neatly separated.
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.2: Transformer is an architecture presented in 2017 in the paper “Attention Is All You Need”. The new idea was to let attention, the mechanism where tokens fetch information from each other, do almost all the work. Everything in this course is a transformer.
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.3: The original was built for translation and had two halves:
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.4: an encoder that reads the whole source text, where every word sees all the others
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.5: a decoder that writes the translation one word at a time and only sees what has already been written
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.6: Decoder-only means keeping only the second half. That is enough to continue text: the prompt and the response are a single sequence, and every token only sees the tokens before it. The GPT and Llama families are built that way.
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.2: The model consists of a single construction, a block (also called a layer), that repeats. The count is called L. Llama-3-8B has L = 32.
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.3: All blocks share the same blueprint: first attention, then the MLP. But each block has its own weights, so they learn to do different things.
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.4: Why stack them? A block can only do one round of “fetch information from other tokens, process it”. Many conclusions need several rounds in a row, where each round builds on the previous one.
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.5: Drag the slider to see what more blocks cost and what they give you.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.1: The shape never changes, until the end
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.2: The stream x has shape [T, 4096]: T rows, one per token, and 4096 numbers per row. That shape holds after the embedding, after every block and after the final norm.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.3: It is a deliberate choice, and it enables three things:
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.4: Blocks can be stacked. What comes out of one block fits straight into the next.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.5: Contributions can be added. x + contribution requires that both have the same shape.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.6: The stream can be read anywhere. After any block it is the same kind of vector, which interpretation methods make use of.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.7: Only in the LM head, the model’s last matrix, does it change form: from 4096 numbers per row to 128,256, one number per token in the vocabulary. More on that in the logits lesson.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.2: The problem. Because every block adds to the stream, x grows in size the deeper you go into the model. Attention and the MLP, however, work best when their input always has roughly the same scale.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.3: The solution is normalization: rescale a vector so that its size (RMS) becomes 1, without changing the direction. The formula comes on the RMSNorm slide.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.4: There are two variants of where to normalize:
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.5: Post-norm (the 2017 original): the stream itself is normalized after every addition.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.6: Pre-norm (Llama and most modern models): the block normalizes a copy before it reads. The stream itself is left untouched and can grow.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.7: Pre-norm makes deep models more stable to train, because the path straight through the stream is never disturbed. The price is that the stream is never normalized along the way, so it must be normalized once at the end, before the LM head. That is the final RMSNorm.
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.10: The curve is an illustration. The stream’s size does grow with depth in pre-norm models, broadly speaking, but exact values vary between models.
n3c.transformer-och-decoder-only.arialab: The original’s encoder and decoder compared with decoder-only
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.arialabe: Stacked blocks. The bar shows how the total parameters split between the L blocks and the two fixed tables, embedding and LM head.
n3c.shapen-andras-aldrig.arialabel: The tensor’s shape at each step through the model
n3c.normalisering-varfor-och-var.arialab: The size of the stream and of what the blocks read, through 32 blocks
n3c.ett-block-staplat-32-ganger.21: Where the parameters sit: each block holds about 0.218 B, so 32 blocks give 6.98 B. Outside the stack there are only two tables — embedding (0.525 B) and LM head (0.525 B). That is 8.03 B in total, with about 87 % in the blocks. The share rises with L but never reaches 100 %, because the two tables keep their size however many blocks you stack. Each extra block also buys less than the one before: the first rounds establish the broad connections, later ones refine them.
